passage:
Monday night. Thunder cracked. From his cot Akash whimpered, then sobbed, clutching the bars. Urmila went straight in, lifted him, and hummed until his breathing slowed.
Wednesday night. Thunder again. A whimper. She came, rubbed his back, and sat by the cot until he slept.
Saturday night. A rumble. One small whimper. Urmila called softly from the doorway, “I'm here, Akash.” He hugged his cloth rabbit and settled on his own.

qa.q: What did Akash hug on Saturday night?
qa.a: He hugged his cloth rabbit.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he whimpered and sobbed on Monday night?
qa.a: He was frightened by the thunder and wanted his mother close; the sobbing and clutching showed distress and a wish for comfort.

qa.q: Why did Urmila's approach work over the week?
qa.a: She soothed him every time instead of ignoring him, so he learned she would come, and by Saturday her voice alone was enough to help him calm down.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel on Saturday night when Akash settles on his own?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and proud that he is learning to calm down.

grounding: It shows a toddler whimpering and clinging after a scare and a parent's consistent soothing helping him learn to calm down.

passage:
At the supermarket checkout in Cape Town, Lindiwe spotted the sweets. Zeynep said, “Not today.”
“NO! NO!” Lindiwe screamed, arching in the trolley seat.
A man behind them muttered, “Just shout louder than her.”
Zeynep didn't. She bent close and spoke low. “You really want sweets. The answer is no. Do you want to hold the bananas or the bread?”
Lindiwe's scream broke into hiccups. She looked at both, then grabbed the bananas.

qa.q: What did Lindiwe choose to hold?
qa.a: Lindiwe grabbed the bananas.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling when she screamed "NO!"?
qa.a: She was angry and felt powerless at being refused the sweets, and screaming was the biggest way to say so without many words.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, the man's or Zeynep's, and why?
qa.a: Zeynep's calm, low voice, clear limit and small choice worked, because it gave Lindiwe some control without giving in; shouting back would likely have made it louder.

qa.q: How did the man behind them see the outburst?
qa.a: He saw it as a contest to win by shouting louder than her.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler screaming no when denied something and a parent using a calm limit and a choice instead of shouting back.

subtype: Screaming and shrieking in play or upset [Expressing]
passage:
I'm Ritu. My little sister Payal shrieks a lot, and it took me ages to work out that her shrieks aren't all the same.
At the splash pool on Sunday she shrieked every time the water hit her, and she was grinning and kicking.
Ten minutes later our cousin grabbed her bucket. Same shriek, but her face went red and her fists shook.
Mummy didn't just hear the noise. She looked at Payal's face and at the bucket, then said, “You're cross! He took it."

qa.q: Where did Payal shriek every time the water hit her?
qa.a: At the splash pool on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling with each shriek?
qa.a: At the splash pool she was delighted, shown by her grin and kicking; when her bucket was taken she was angry, shown by her red face and shaking fists.

qa.q: How did Mummy work out what Payal's shriek meant?
qa.a: She looked at Payal's face and what had just happened with the bucket, instead of judging by the sound alone.

qa.q: What was confusing for Ritu about Payal's shrieks?
qa.a: The sound was the same whether Payal was happy or cross, so Ritu had to watch her face and the situation to tell.

grounding: It shows a toddler shrieking in delight and screaming in frustration, with a caregiver reading her face and the setting to tell which.

passage:
Notes for Jahnavi's parents, Wednesday. From Sarita Aunty.
She pushed the little stool across the floor all by herself this morning, grunting with every shove, “Hnh! Hnh!” I said, “Pushing hard!”
Before her nap she flopped on the mat and gave a long sigh, so I knew she was ready.
After waking she sat with her doll humming “mmm-mmm-mmm.” I hummed it back and she giggled and hummed again 😊.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi push across the floor?
qa.a: She pushed the little stool across the floor.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi's humming with her doll suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt content and relaxed after her nap, and the giggle when Sarita hummed back shows she enjoyed sharing it.

qa.q: How does Sarita support Jahnavi's language?
qa.a: By echoing her sounds warmly, like humming back and saying "Pushing hard!", Sarita turns her grunts and hums into a shared conversation.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would probably feel reassured that Sarita notices Jahnavi's small sounds and responds warmly.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler grunting with effort, sighing when tired and humming when content, with a caregiver echoing the sounds warmly.

passage:
In the Chandigarh flat, Jomon, who babysits on Fridays, poured Gurpreet some mango juice.
Gurpreet knocked the cup. “Uh-oh!”
“Uh-oh, spilled,” said Jomon calmly, and grabbed a cloth.
Gurpreet sipped his refilled cup. “Ahh!”
“Yummy? You like mango.”
Then a green parrot landed on the balcony rail. Gurpreet's mouth made a round “Oh!”
“Oh! A surprise!” Jomon whispered. “A parrot!"

qa.q: What landed on the balcony rail?
qa.a: A green parrot landed on the balcony rail.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when he said "Oh!" at the parrot?
qa.a: He was surprised and interested, and his round mouth and "Oh!" shared that with Jomon.

qa.q: How does Jomon help Gurpreet build words?
qa.a: Jomon answers each short sound calmly with a name for the event or feeling, like "spilled," "yummy" and "surprise."

qa.q: How might Jomon feel when Gurpreet says "Uh-oh!" at the spill?
qa.a: Jomon likely feels calm, even amused, since Gurpreet is noticing and sharing what happened rather than hiding it.

grounding: It shows a toddler saying uh-oh, ah and oh at a spill, a taste and a surprise, and an adult responding with calm names for them.

subtype: Baby talk and rising pitch from adults [Interpreting]
passage:
“Lokesh. Come here,” said Dadu, low and flat, from his chair.
Lokesh stopped playing and stared, worried, not moving.
Madhuri laughed. “Lo-KESH! Come see Dadu!” she sang, her voice going up and up.
Lokesh's face lit up and he toddled over.
“Why does he come for you and not for me?” asked Dadu.
“He's not scared of you, Papa. Your voice just sounds serious to him. Try it singing.”
“Lo-kesh!” Dadu tried, higher. Lokesh climbed onto his knee.

qa.q: Where was Dadu sitting when he called Lokesh?
qa.a: He was sitting in his chair.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when Dadu called in a low, flat voice?
qa.a: He seemed worried and unsure, perhaps thinking he was in trouble, because the flat voice sounded serious to him.

qa.q: What small change helped Dadu connect with Lokesh?
qa.a: Using a higher, sing-song voice, which Lokesh reads as warm and inviting.

qa.q: How did Dadu feel when Lokesh ran to Madhuri's call instead of his?
qa.a: Dadu seemed puzzled and a little hurt, asking why Lokesh came for her and not for him.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler reading a sing-song, rising voice as warm and a low, flat voice as serious, before understanding the words.

passage:
“Higher, Appa! Higher!” Sudha squealed on the swing, loud and bright.
“She'll wake the whole colony,” said Amma, laughing.
That night Sudha lay murmuring low to her doll, “mm, baby, mm.”
“Sleepy voice,” whispered Chaitanya.
The next morning a sudden scream came from the hall, high and sharp.
Chaitanya ran. “That's not her happy scream.”
Sudha was holding her finger by the door hinge. He checked it, no cut, just red. “Ouch, it's pinched. Come here."

qa.q: What was Sudha doing on the swing?
qa.a: She was squealing "Higher, Appa! Higher!" loud and bright.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she screamed high and sharp in the morning?
qa.a: She was in sudden pain and frightened after pinching her finger in the door hinge, which sounded different from her usual happy squeals.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do well when he heard the scream?
qa.a: He noticed the change from her usual loud sounds, went at once and checked her finger before comforting her.

qa.q: How does Amma see Sudha's loud squeals on the swing?
qa.a: Amma finds them funny and joyful, joking that she'll wake the whole colony.

grounding: It shows a toddler's loud high voice in excitement, low murmur when sleepy, and a sudden change of pitch that signals pain.

passage:
In the Lisbon flat, Noa tiptoed up to the pram where her baby cousin was sleeping.
“Ba-by,” she breathed, so softly it was almost air, her eyes wide.
“Yes, sleeping baby,” whispered her father, Rafael.
That afternoon, a neighbour knocked with a cake. Noa slipped behind Rafael's legs and breathed, “Hi,” barely audible, face half hidden.
“She's a bit shy,” Rafael said. “Give her time."

qa.q: What did the neighbour bring?
qa.a: The neighbour knocked with a cake.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling when she breathed "Ba-by" by the pram?
qa.a: She seemed full of wonder and was being careful and quiet around the sleeping baby, which is why her voice was hushed.

qa.q: How did Rafael read Noa's breathy voice correctly both times?
qa.a: He looked at the context: by the pram it was gentle politeness and awe, and behind his legs with a hidden face it was shyness.

qa.q: How might the neighbour feel about Noa's whispered "Hi"?
qa.a: The neighbour would probably understand she was shy and feel pleased she said hello at all.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler's breathy, whispery voice carrying awe and politeness near a sleeping baby and shyness when hiding from a visitor.

passage:
The Delhi metro was packed. Pankaj held Ira's hand as more people pushed in.
“Pa-pa,” she said, and her voice wobbled, thin and choked. Her chin started to shake.
Pankaj heard it. He didn't wait for the tears. He lifted her onto his hip, turned his back to the crowd and spoke slow and low. “I've got you. Big crowd. We're safe here.”
Ira pressed her face into his neck. Her breath caught twice, then steadied.

qa.q: Where was Pankaj holding Ira's hand?
qa.a: He was holding Ira's hand in the packed Delhi metro.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when her voice wobbled and choked?
qa.a: She was frightened and overwhelmed by the pushing crowd and was close to crying.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj's quick response help?
qa.a: He answered the wobble in her voice early, lifting her close and speaking calmly, which stopped the fear from turning into a full meltdown.

qa.q: What would change if Pankaj had waited for Ira to start crying?
qa.a: She might have had a full meltdown in the crowded carriage, which would be harder to calm.

grounding: It shows a toddler's trembling, choked voice signalling fear in a crowd, and a caregiver answering it early with calm and closeness.

passage:
Nanny's note, Thursday. From Nirmala.
At the park, Swati chattered fast, “ba-da-ba-da-ba!”, running to the swings and pointing.
By five she had slowed down. Just one word at a time, then nothing, leaning on my knee.
At home she sat with her blocks going “ma-ma-ma-ma” over and over. Her mother came in thinking she was calling. I think it's just her playing sound, happy and settled.

qa.q: Where did Swati chatter fast?
qa.a: At the park, running to the swings.

qa.q: What did Swati's slow, stopping speech at five suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she was tired after the park, which is why she leaned on Nirmala's knee.

qa.q: How could Swati's mother respond to the "ma-ma-ma" next time?
qa.a: She could enjoy it as play and comfort, smiling or joining the rhythm, rather than assuming Swati is calling her.

qa.q: How did Swati's mother read the "ma-ma-ma" sounds?
qa.a: She thought Swati was calling her, though it was more likely a happy playing sound.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler babbling fast when excited, slowing when tired, and repeating syllables in play as comfort rather than words.
